title: The Model Assistant in action: What would an escalating Iran war mean for bond yields?
gist: Oxford Economics uses its AI Model Assistant to run a renewed Iran-war escalation scenario through its Global Economic Model: +$37 Brent, higher European/Asian gas prices and supply-chain stress from 2026Q4-2027Q4 push US 10-year yields 0.78pp above baseline at the peak in 2028Q2. Adding a more hawkish Fed (+50bp) makes yields rise faster and stay higher for longer.

themes.theme: Current market backdrop of the Iran war

insights.claim: Renewed attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure in the Gulf during the Iran war have lifted oil prices and triggered a sharp global bond market sell-off.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Geopolitical energy shock is already transmitting into global duration risk.
insights.quote: Renewed attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure in the Gulf have lifted oil prices, and global bond markets have sold off sharply.

insights.claim: As of October 2026, the US 10-year Treasury yield has climbed above 5% for the first time since 2007, and the Federal Reserve raised rates in September 2026 for the first time since 2023.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: The Fed has pivoted back to hiking and long yields are at multi-decade highs, a regime shift for rates positioning.
insights.quote: The US 10-year Treasury yield has climbed above 5% for the first time since 2007
insights.locator: The war in Iran has already

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' baseline forecast already incorporates the Iran conflict and market moves to date, so the escalation scenario measures additional upside risk on top of an already-stressed baseline.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Scenario deltas are incremental to a baseline that already has 5%+ 10-year yields.
insights.quote: Our baseline forecast already reflects the conflict and the market moves seen so far.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' downside case for a prolonged Iran war points to sustained energy disruption, higher inflation risk premia and increased long-term borrowing costs.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Identifies the channels (energy, inflation premia, term premia) through which escalation hits bonds.
insights.quote: sustained energy disruption, higher inflation risk premia and increased long-term borrowing costs

insights.claim: The escalation scenario assumes Brent crude $37 above baseline, European gas +$5, Asian gas +$10, and supply chain stress +1.0, all from 2026Q4 to 2027Q4.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Gives concrete stress-test magnitudes for energy and logistics exposure in a sustained-war case.

insights.claim: In a prolonged Iran-war disruption, Asian gas prices are assumed to rise twice as much as European gas prices because Asian LNG markets are more exposed to prolonged disruption.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Suggests Asian LNG importers carry greater energy-shock risk than Europe in a Gulf escalation.
insights.quote: Asian LNG markets’ greater exposure to prolonged disruption

insights.claim: In Oxford Economics' Iran-escalation scenario, US 10-year government bond yields peak 0.78 percentage points above baseline in 2028Q2.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: With yields already above 5%, escalation could push the 10-year toward ~5.8%, with the peak gap arriving well after the shock window.
insights.quote: US 10-year government bond yields are 0.78 percentage points above baseline at their widest gap, in 2028Q2

insights.claim: In the escalation scenario, higher energy prices and supply-chain stress create inflation pressure that prompts tighter monetary policy, keeping risk premia elevated, lifting yields and tightening financial conditions.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Energy shock is bearish duration via both inflation and policy channels, while tightening financial conditions for risk assets.

insights.claim: The Fed faces a stagflationary trade-off in an energy shock: higher inflation pushes it to raise rates first, while weaker growth and a softer labour market subsequently lead to rate cuts, a Taylor-rule mechanism embedded in the Global Economic Model.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Implies a hike-then-cut policy path, relevant for timing front-end versus long-end rates trades.
insights.quote: Higher inflation creates pressure to raise rates, while weaker growth and a softer labour market subsequently lead to rate cuts.

insights.claim: If the Fed is assumed more hawkish, holding the policy rate 50bp above baseline from 2026Q4 to 2027Q4 until the energy shock fades, US bond yields rise more quickly and stay higher for longer than in the base escalation scenario.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A hawkish Fed response amplifies rather than caps long-end yield upside in an energy shock.
insights.quote: With a more hawkish Fed, US bond yields rise more quickly and stay higher for longer than in our first run.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' AskOEAI Model Assistant, billed as the world's first AI assistant for scenario modelling, can turn a plain-language prompt into calibrated shocks, solve them through the Global Economic Model, and benchmark results against the baseline without the user specifying variables or shock sizes.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Lowers the cost of macro scenario analysis, democratising stress-testing that previously required model expertise; sold as a GEM add-on.
insights.quote: We didn’t need to know which variables to shock, by how much, or how to set up the model inputs.
insights.locator: From economic question to modelled insight
